title: Security Monitoring & Log Analysis
description: Read auth, Windows, web, and DNS logs and SIEM queries to separate real attacks from noise.

questions.prompt: A Linux web server's /var/log/auth.log contains the lines below. What is the correct conclusion?

code.source:
Feb 12 02:11:41 web01 sshd[4182]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.77 port 51122 ssh2
Feb 12 02:11:43 web01 sshd[4182]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.77 port 51122 ssh2
Feb 12 02:11:46 web01 sshd[4190]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.77 port 51130 ssh2
... 309 similar lines from 203.0.113.77 over the next 9 minutes ...
Feb 12 02:20:58 web01 sshd[5007]: Accepted password for root from 203.0.113.77 port 52610 ssh2
Feb 12 02:20:58 web01 sshd[5007]: pam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for user root(uid=0) by (uid=0)

options.text: The attack failed, since failed attempts far outnumber successful ones
An administrator forgot the root password and eventually remembered it
A brute-force attack on root over SSH succeeded; treat the host as compromised
A password spray across many accounts that only reached the root account

questions.explanation: Hundreds of rapid failures for one account from one IP, followed by an Accepted password and an opened session from that same IP, is a successful brute force (MITRE ATT&CK T1110.001). What matters is the final success, not the ratio of failures to successes.

questions.prompt: You are building a SIEM rule that alerts whenever a new user account is created on a Windows domain controller or member server. Which Windows Security log event ID should the rule match?
questions.explanation: Event 4720 is "A user account was created." 4624 and 4625 are successful and failed logons, and 4688 is process creation. Matching 4624 would alert on every logon instead of on account creation.

questions.prompt: These Apache access log entries come from one client. What do they show?

options.text: Routine traffic; every request except one returned 200, so nothing was exploited
Automated SQL injection probing; the size change between 1=1 and 1=2 suggests id is injectable
A denial-of-service attempt, because the 500 response shows the server crashed
A crawler requesting product pages that don't exist on the site

questions.explanation: The sqlmap user agent, the quote that triggers a 500 error, and the boolean pair AND 1=1 (full 5120-byte page) versus AND 1=2 (210 bytes) are classic boolean-based SQL injection testing, and the differing responses suggest the parameter is vulnerable. A 200 status means the server answered, not that the request was safe.

questions.prompt: Firewall logs are recorded in UTC. An application server in Denver writes local time (Mountain Standard Time, UTC-7, no daylight saving in February). The server logged a suspicious login at 09:15 on February 10. What firewall timestamp should you search around?
questions.explanation: Local time = UTC - 7, so UTC = 09:15 + 7 h = 16:15. Subtracting the offset gives 02:15 (the wrong direction), and 15:15 comes from applying the daylight-saving offset (UTC-6) that isn't in effect in February.

questions.prompt: True or false: In a Linux auth.log, the line "Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.4" means the account admin exists on the system but the password was wrong.
questions.explanation: OpenSSH logs "invalid user" when the username does not exist on the host. A wrong password for a real account is logged as "Failed password for admin". Telling the two apart shows whether an attacker is guessing usernames or attacking real accounts.

questions.prompt: A SIEM search returns these Windows events from a domain controller (420 accounts in total, one attempt each, over 14 minutes). What is the most accurate assessment?

options.text: Password spraying (T1110.003) with one success; treat e.walsh as compromised
Brute force (T1110.001) aimed at a single privileged account
A lockout storm from stale credentials cached on a service host
Kerberoasting (T1558.003) to request service tickets for offline cracking

questions.explanation: One source trying a single password across many accounts is password spraying. The 4624 for e.walsh from the same IP means one guess worked. Sub status 0xC0000064 (user does not exist) also shows the attacker is working from a guessed username list, which stale service credentials would not produce.

questions.prompt: This PostgreSQL query should list source IPs with more than 20 failed logins in the last hour, worst first. Which line causes it to fail?

code.source:
SELECT src_ip, COUNT(*) AS failures
FROM auth_events
WHERE outcome = 'failure'
  AND event_time >= NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour'
GROUP BY src_ip
WHERE COUNT(*) > 20
ORDER BY failures DESC;

questions.explanation: Filters on aggregates must go in HAVING (HAVING COUNT(*) > 20), and a second WHERE after GROUP BY is a syntax error. The first WHERE clause is correct because it filters individual rows before grouping.

questions.prompt: This event appears on APP-SRV-03, an internal database server. What kind of access does it record, and why is it a concern?

code.source:
Event ID: 4624  An account was successfully logged on.
TimeCreated:            2026-06-18 03:12:44
Logon Type:             10
Account Name:           svc_sql
Workstation Name:       DESKTOP-K7Q2L9
Source Network Address: 203.0.113.211
Logon Process:          User32
Authentication Package: Negotiate

options.text: A network logon to a file share, which is normal for a service account that reads files
An interactive RDP session from an internet address using a service account, which should never happen
A scheduled task running as svc_sql, which suggests an attacker created persistence on the server
A service starting under svc_sql after a reboot, which only matters if the reboot was unplanned

questions.explanation: Logon Type 10 is RemoteInteractive (RDP/Terminal Services). Type 3 is network, 4 is batch (scheduled tasks), and 5 is service. A service account logging on interactively from a public IP at 03:12 points to stolen credentials and exposed RDP.

questions.prompt: A WordPress server's access log shows the entries below. What happened, and what should the analyst do?

options.text: Normal thumbnail generation, since PHP scripts in uploads return 200 responses
A failed directory traversal attempt, since the responses are small and nothing changed
An unauthenticated plugin scan that found nothing, so the source IP should just be blocked
A web shell (T1505.003) running OS commands; treat the server as compromised and contain it

questions.explanation: A PHP file uploaded into the uploads directory and then called with commands such as whoami and cat /etc/passwd, returning 200 with output-sized responses, is a working web shell. The host needs containment and investigation (including how the upload got through), not just an IP block.

questions.prompt: These entries come from the internal DNS resolver's query log. Select the TWO observations that point to DNS tunneling (T1071.004).

code.source:
10:41:02 client=10.0.3.51 type=TXT  q=a3f9c1e07b2d4e58a91f0c6d3b7e2a14f8c9.t1.example.net
10:41:03 client=10.0.3.51 type=TXT  q=5e8b2c71f0a94d36b1e7c28a0f5d9b3c6e1a.t1.example.net
10:41:03 client=10.0.3.51 type=TXT  q=b07d4e19a2c85f63e0b9d17c4a2f8e6b3d05.t1.example.net
10:41:04 client=10.0.3.51 type=TXT  q=9c2e5a08d7f14b3e6a0c9d28b5f17e4a3c62.t1.example.net
10:41:05 client=10.0.3.51 type=A    q=outlook.office365.com
10:41:05 client=10.0.3.51 type=TXT  q=e41b7d0a3c95f28e1b6d4a07c3e9f52b8d17.t1.example.net

options.text: Long, high-entropy subdomain labels that are different on every query
Rapid, repeated TXT queries to subdomains of a single parent domain
The client also resolved outlook.office365.com with an A query
The client is an internal 10.x address rather than a public one
The queries go to the corporate resolver on port 53

questions.explanation: Tunnels encode data in unique, random-looking subdomain labels and often use TXT records to carry return data, producing bursts of queries to one domain. Querying Office 365, having an internal IP, and using the corporate resolver on port 53 are all normal.

questions.prompt: You need to detect powershell.exe launched with -EncodedCommand on Windows endpoints. No EDR or Sysmon is deployed. What logging must be in place for the SIEM to see this?

options.text: Event 4688 (process creation) with "Include command line in process creation events" enabled
Event 4624 logon events with Logon Type recorded for every interactive session
Windows Firewall logs of outbound connections from powershell.exe
DHCP server logs that map each endpoint's IP address to its hostname

questions.explanation: Event 4688 only records the full command line, which is where -EncodedCommand appears, when that policy setting is enabled (PowerShell script block logging, event 4104, is another option). Logon and firewall events never show process arguments.

questions.prompt: Within 30 seconds, a domain controller logged the 4769 events summarized below, all requested by one standard user from a workstation. What is the most likely activity, and which control most reduces its impact?

code.source:
EventID  Account          ServiceName    TicketEncryptionType  ClientAddress
4769     j.doe@CORP.LCL   svc_sql        0x17                  ::ffff:10.0.6.44
4769     j.doe@CORP.LCL   svc_backup     0x17                  ::ffff:10.0.6.44
4769     j.doe@CORP.LCL   svc_sharepoint 0x17                  ::ffff:10.0.6.44
4769     j.doe@CORP.LCL   svc_reporting  0x17                  ::ffff:10.0.6.44
... 11 more distinct service accounts, all 0x17 ...

options.text: Golden ticket use; reset the KRBTGT password twice
AS-REP roasting; require Kerberos pre-authentication on all accounts
Kerberoasting; give service accounts long random or gMSA-managed passwords
Normal service access; 4769 is routine, so tune these events out of the SIEM

questions.explanation: One user requesting RC4 (0x17) service tickets for many SPNs in seconds is Kerberoasting (T1558.003): the tickets are cracked offline to recover service-account passwords. A long random or gMSA-managed password makes cracking infeasible whatever the cipher; disabling RC4 only slows cracking, so a weak password stays the real exposure. AS-REP roasting shows up as 4768 events against accounts with pre-authentication disabled, not as 4769.

questions.prompt: DC01 logged the event below. Correlated 4624 events show helpdesk-adm logged on to DC01 over the network from 10.0.8.57, a user workstation. What does this most likely indicate?

code.source:
Event ID: 4662  An operation was performed on an object.
Subject Account Name:  helpdesk-adm
Object Server:         DS
Object Type:           domainDNS
Object Name:           DC=corp,DC=lcl
Accesses:              Control Access
Properties:            {1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2}
                       {1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2}

options.text: Routine AD replication between domain controllers using a delegated account
DCSync (T1003.006); assume every domain credential hash has been exposed
Kerberoasting (T1558.003) against service accounts that have registered SPNs
A Group Policy refresh in which the workstation read the domain object

questions.explanation: Those two GUIDs are DS-Replication-Get-Changes and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All. Exercising them from a non-DC host with a user account is the DCSync technique, which pulls password hashes, including KRBTGT's. Real DC-to-DC replication comes from domain controller computer accounts, not from a helpdesk account on a workstation.

questions.prompt: A file server forwards its Security log to the SIEM in near real time. The last events received are shown below, and the server is still running. What is the correct interpretation?

code.source:
02:13:40  4720  A user account was created.  Target: backup_svc2  Subject: j.admin
02:13:52  4732  Member added to security-enabled local group Administrators: backup_svc2
02:14:07  1102  The audit log was cleared.  Subject: j.admin
--- no further Security events received from FS-01 ---

options.text: The log reached its maximum size and rolled over, which is normal housekeeping
The SIEM forwarder crashed, so restart the agent and carry on with routine triage
Event 1102 is expected after patching, because Windows resets its logs during updates
Someone cleared the Security log (T1070.001); rely on copies already forwarded and other sources

questions.explanation: Event 1102 means "The audit log was cleared" and records who did it. Here an admin-level account cleared it right after creating an account, which is classic anti-forensics. Normal rollover does not produce 1102, and the events already forwarded to the SIEM are now the authoritative record.

questions.prompt: A correlation rule runs every 5 minutes and searches the previous 5 minutes by event timestamp. An attack event stamped 10:02:10 arrived in the SIEM at 10:09:45 because of forwarder queuing, and the rule never fired. Why was it missed, and what fixes it?

options.text: Ingestion lag put it outside every window; search by index time or use an overlapping lookback
The rule logic is wrong; rewrite it against the raw event instead of the parsed fields
The event was a duplicate; deduplicate data at the forwarder before indexing
The window is too long; run every minute over a 1-minute event-time window

questions.explanation: At the 10:05 run the event hadn't arrived yet, and the 10:10 run only covered 10:05-10:10 by event time, so the event fell between runs. Searching on index or ingest time, or adding an overlapping lookback with deduplication, closes the gap. Shorter windows make the problem worse.
